		Net migration has dropped. 	
Net migration has fallen into the tens of thousands of people for the first time this century outside of the pandemic, official data has shown, as young Brits leaving the country made up about a fifth of total emigration.

Migration levels dropped to 77,000 in the year to June 2026, estimates by the Office for National Statistics showed.

This represented the lowest level of migration since 1997 outside of the pandemic.

Statisticians said the fall in the net migration of non-EU nationals was the main reason for the decrease.

Immigration of people outside of the EU dropped by more than 100,000 after tougher rules on visas, including higher salary thresholds for workers, limited people from around the world from moving to the UK.

Three daily briefings with the key market moves and top business and political stories.

Total immigration of non-EU nationals in the 12-month period was 550,000, compared to 79,000 for EU nationals and 109,000 for Britons arriving.

Emigration levels of about 661,000 helped bring the net migration figure down significantly. In the previous 12-month period, net migration was at 204,000.

The figures will likely relieve Labour government figures as immigration concerns have been pushed down the list of the British public’s voting priorities in recent months.

For years, the previous Tory government pledged to bring net migration down to the tens of thousands although figures peaked at about 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

Separate Home Office figures showed on Thursday that the number of people claiming asylum dropped by 33 per cent in one year although there were record high numbers in applications for British citizenship.

But official data showed that about 19 per cent of total emigration came from British nationals aged between 16 and 34 leaving the country.

About 65,000 people aged between 25 and 34 left in the 12-month period. Young adults between the age of 16 and 34 made up about half of the total number of British emigrants.

According to the official body, the net outflow of those aged between 25 and 34 has grown by about five times since 2022. The difference has been driven by British nationals choosing not to return to the country.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said that “British and European people are leaving in their droves” due to a higher tax burden.

“The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government,” Philp said.

“We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by Parliament, at a far lower level.

“Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society.”
